lesson.title: Enzyme Inhibition: Competitive, Noncompetitive, and Uncompetitive Mechanisms
lesson.description: Distinguishes among the major classes of enzyme inhibition, explaining how each type alters Km and Vmax and how inhibitors are identified using kinetic data and Lineweaver-Burk plots.
lesson.content:
# Enzyme Inhibition: Competitive, Noncompetitive, and Uncompetitive Mechanisms

## Overview and MCAT Relevance

Enzyme inhibition sits at the intersection of biochemistry, pharmacology, and physiology—three domains the MCAT tests heavily. Nearly every clinically relevant drug works by inhibiting an enzyme: statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase, and penicillin inhibits transpeptidase. Understanding *how* these inhibitors work at the molecular level, and how their effects manifest in kinetic data, is essential for both the Biochemistry section and for reasoning through passage-based questions about drug mechanisms.

The MCAT expects you to do three things fluently: (1) predict how an inhibitor changes **Km** and **Vmax**, (2) identify inhibitor type from a Lineweaver-Burk plot, and (3) connect inhibition type to physiological or pharmacological context. This lesson builds all three skills systematically.

---

## Foundational Kinetics: Km and Vmax Refresher

Before dissecting inhibition types, you need a firm grip on what Km and Vmax mean, because inhibitors are defined entirely by how they perturb these parameters.

**Vmax** is the maximum reaction velocity achieved when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate. It is directly proportional to the total enzyme concentration: Vmax = kcat × [E]total. *Vmax changes only when the effective amount of catalytically competent enzyme changes.*

**Km** (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration at which reaction velocity equals ½ Vmax. It reflects the affinity between enzyme and substrate: a *low* Km means high affinity (enzyme reaches half-saturation at low [S]), while a *high* Km means low affinity. Importantly, Km is an apparent constant—anything that makes it harder to saturate the enzyme with substrate will raise the apparent Km.

The **Michaelis-Menten equation** is:

v = (Vmax × [S]) / (Km + [S])

This equation describes a hyperbolic curve. At low [S], velocity is approximately linear with [S]. At high [S], velocity plateaus at Vmax. Inhibitors distort this curve in characteristic ways.

### The Lineweaver-Burk Plot

Because hyperbolic curves are hard to analyze visually, biochemists use the **Lineweaver-Burk plot** (double-reciprocal plot), which linearizes the Michaelis-Menten equation by taking the reciprocal of both sides:

1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax

This is a line in the form y = mx + b, where:
- The **y-intercept** = 1/Vmax
- The **x-intercept** = −1/Km
- The **slope** = Km/Vmax

Every inhibitor type produces a characteristic change to this line. Mastering these graphical signatures is one of the highest-yield skills for MCAT biochemistry.

---

## Competitive Inhibition

### Molecular Mechanism

A **competitive inhibitor** is a molecule that binds reversibly to the enzyme's *active site*—the same site where substrate normally binds. Because the inhibitor and substrate compete for the same binding pocket, their binding is mutually exclusive: when the inhibitor is bound, substrate cannot bind, and vice versa.

The key structural feature is that competitive inhibitors are typically *structural analogs* of the substrate. Methotrexate, for example, resembles dihydrofolate closely enough to occupy the active site of dihydrofolate reductase with very high affinity, blocking the enzyme's ability to reduce folate to tetrahydrofolate—a step essential for nucleotide synthesis.

The equilibrium can be written as:

E + I ⇌ EI (inhibitor binds active site)
E + S ⇌ ES → E + P (normal catalysis)

The inhibitor constant **Ki** describes the dissociation of the EI complex: Ki = [E][I]/[EI]. A smaller Ki means the inhibitor binds more tightly.

### Effect on Km and Vmax

This is the most tested aspect of competitive inhibition:

- **Vmax: unchanged**
- **Apparent Km: increased**

The reasoning is intuitive. Because the inhibitor and substrate compete, adding more substrate can *outcompete* the inhibitor—at sufficiently high [S], essentially all enzyme active sites will be occupied by substrate, and the inhibitor's effect is overcome. This means the enzyme can still reach the same maximum velocity; it just requires more substrate to get there. The apparent Km increases by the factor α = 1 + [I]/Ki.

The modified Michaelis-Menten equation under competitive inhibition becomes:

v = Vmax × [S] / (αKm + [S])

where α = 1 + [I]/Ki. Note that α > 1 always, so αKm > Km.

### Lineweaver-Burk Signature

On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, competitive inhibition produces:
- **Same y-intercept** (1/Vmax is unchanged)
- **Different x-intercept** (−1/αKm is less negative, i.e., shifted right toward zero)
- **Steeper slope** (slope = αKm/Vmax increases)

Visually, the inhibited line *pivots around the y-intercept*—the lines intersect on the y-axis. This is the definitive graphical signature of competitive inhibition.

### Clinical Example: Statins

Statins (e.g., lovastatin, atorvastatin) competitively inhibit **HMG-CoA reductase**, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. Statins are structural analogs of the natural substrate HMG-CoA, binding the active site with much higher affinity than the substrate itself. This reduces hepatic cholesterol synthesis, upregulates LDL receptors, and lowers plasma LDL—a classic competitive inhibition with profound clinical impact.

---

## Noncompetitive Inhibition

### Molecular Mechanism

A **noncompetitive inhibitor** binds to a site *other than* the active site, called an **allosteric site** (or regulatory site). Critically, the inhibitor can bind whether or not substrate is already occupying the active site. This means:

- E + I ⇌ EI (inhibitor binds free enzyme)
- ES + I ⇌ ESI (inhibitor binds enzyme-substrate complex)
- The inhibitor binds with equal affinity to E and ES

Because the inhibitor does not block substrate binding, the enzyme-substrate complex can still form. However, the ESI complex is *catalytically inactive*—the inhibitor's binding induces a conformational change that impairs the enzyme's ability to convert substrate to product.

### Effect on Km and Vmax

- **Vmax: decreased**
- **Km: unchanged**

The decrease in Vmax occurs because a fraction of enzyme molecules are permanently tied up in the inactive ESI complex regardless of how much substrate is added. Unlike competitive inhibition, you cannot overcome noncompetitive inhibition by flooding the system with substrate—the inhibitor will bind to ES complexes just as readily as to free enzyme.

Km remains unchanged because the inhibitor does not affect the enzyme's affinity for substrate. Substrate can still bind just as well; it just cannot be converted to product as efficiently.

The modified equation becomes:

v = (Vmax/α) × [S] / (Km + [S])

where α = 1 + [I]/Ki. The apparent Vmax is reduced to Vmax/α, while Km stays the same.

### Lineweaver-Burk Signature

On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, noncompetitive inhibition produces:
- **Higher y-intercept** (1/Vmax increases because Vmax decreases)
- **Same x-intercept** (−1/Km unchanged)
- **Steeper slope** (slope = Km/Vmax increases because Vmax decreases)

Visually, the inhibited line intersects the uninhibited line *on the x-axis*. This x-axis intersection is the definitive signature of pure noncompetitive inhibition.

### Mixed Inhibition: A Nuance

*Pure* noncompetitive inhibition (equal affinity for E and ES) is actually rare. More commonly, an inhibitor binds to an allosteric site but with *different* affinities for E versus ES. This is called **mixed inhibition**. In mixed inhibition:

- **Vmax decreases** (α > 1 affects Vmax)
- **Km changes** (either increases or decreases depending on whether the inhibitor prefers E or ES)

On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, mixed inhibition lines intersect *in the second quadrant* (to the left of the y-axis, above or below the x-axis). The MCAT most commonly tests pure noncompetitive inhibition, but recognizing that "noncompetitive" and "mixed" are sometimes used interchangeably in older texts is worth noting.

### Clinical Example: Cyanide Poisoning

Cyanide (CN⁻) is a classic noncompetitive inhibitor of **cytochrome c oxidase** (Complex IV of the electron transport chain). Cyanide binds to the iron center of cytochrome c oxidase at a site that is not the substrate (cytochrome c) binding site. It binds regardless of whether cytochrome c is present, and it completely inactivates the enzyme. This halts oxidative phosphorylation, causing rapid cellular asphyxiation even in the presence of oxygen—a lethal consequence of noncompetitive inhibition.

---

## Uncompetitive Inhibition

### Molecular Mechanism

**Uncompetitive inhibition** is the least intuitive of the three types and is often the most poorly understood by students. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds *exclusively to the enzyme-substrate complex (ES)*—it cannot bind to free enzyme.

E + S ⇌ ES → E + P (normal)
ES + I ⇌ ESI (inhibitor binds only ES)

This means the inhibitor requires substrate to be present before it can bind. The ESI complex is a dead-end complex—it cannot proceed to form product.

### Effect on Km and Vmax

This is where uncompetitive inhibition becomes counterintuitive:

- **Vmax: decreased**
- **Apparent Km: decreased**

Both Km and Vmax decrease by the *same factor* (α' = 1 + [I]/Ki'), which means their *ratio* (Km/Vmax) stays constant.

Why does Km decrease? When the inhibitor sequesters ES into the inactive ESI complex, it effectively removes ES from the equilibrium. By Le Chatelier's principle, the enzyme-substrate equilibrium shifts to the right to replenish ES—meaning the enzyme binds substrate *more readily* than it would without inhibitor. The apparent Km falls.

Why does Vmax decrease? Despite the increased substrate affinity, the ESI complex is catalytically dead. A fraction of enzyme is permanently locked in ESI, reducing the effective enzyme concentration available for catalysis. No amount of additional substrate can rescue this—adding more substrate actually drives more ESI formation.

The modified equations are:

Apparent Km = Km/α'
Apparent Vmax = Vmax/α'

where α' = 1 + [I]/Ki'.

### Lineweaver-Burk Signature

This is the most distinctive graphical signature:
- **Higher y-intercept** (1/Vmax increases)
- **x-intercept shifts right** (−1/Km becomes less negative because Km decreases)
- **Same slope** (slope = Km/Vmax is unchanged because both decrease equally)

On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the inhibited and uninhibited lines are **parallel**—they never intersect. This parallel-line pattern is the unmistakable signature of uncompetitive inhibition. No other inhibition type produces parallel lines.

### Clinical Relevance

Uncompetitive inhibition is less common in single-substrate reactions but appears frequently in multi-substrate enzyme systems. **Lithium**, used to treat bipolar disorder, acts as an uncompetitive inhibitor of **inositol monophosphatase**, an enzyme involved in the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway. By selectively inhibiting the enzyme only when it is substrate-bound, lithium's effect is greatest in neurons that are most active (highest substrate turnover)—a pharmacologically elegant consequence of uncompetitive inhibition.

---

## Irreversible Inhibition

While the three major types above are all *reversible*, the MCAT also tests **irreversible inhibition**, which deserves a focused discussion.

An **irreversible inhibitor** forms a covalent bond with the enzyme, permanently inactivating it. The enzyme cannot be reactivated; recovery of enzyme activity requires synthesis of new enzyme protein.

### Key Features

- Irreversible inhibitors are sometimes called **suicide inhibitors** or **mechanism-based inhibitors** when they are activated by the enzyme's own catalytic machinery before forming the covalent bond.
- Because enzyme is permanently inactivated, the effect on Vmax is a *reduction* that cannot be reversed by adding more substrate.
- Km is typically unchanged (the inhibitor doesn't affect affinity of remaining active enzyme for substrate).
- The degree of inhibition depends on the *concentration of inhibitor* and *time of exposure*, not on substrate concentration.

### Clinical Examples

- **Aspirin** irreversibly acetylates a serine residue in the active site of **cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2)**, permanently inhibiting prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis. Platelets, lacking nuclei, cannot synthesize new COX—so a single aspirin dose inhibits platelet COX for the platelet's entire 7–10 day lifespan.
- **Organophosphates** (nerve agents, some pesticides) irreversibly phosphorylate the serine in the active site of **acetylcholinesterase**, preventing breakdown of acetylcholine at synapses. This causes continuous nerve stimulation—a lethal consequence.
- **Penicillin** irreversibly inhibits **transpeptidase** (penicillin-binding proteins) by forming a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate, blocking bacterial cell wall synthesis.

---

## Comparative Summary Table

The following summary organizes the key kinetic changes for rapid review:

**Competitive Inhibition**
- Binds: Active site (free enzyme only)
- Km: Increased (αKm)
- Vmax: Unchanged
- Lineweaver-Burk: Lines intersect at y-axis
- Overcome by substrate? Yes

**Noncompetitive Inhibition**
- Binds: Allosteric site (E and ES equally)
- Km: Unchanged
- Vmax: Decreased (Vmax/α)
- Lineweaver-Burk: Lines intersect at x-axis
- Overcome by substrate? No

**Uncompetitive Inhibition**
- Binds: Allosteric site (ES only)
- Km: Decreased (Km/α')
- Vmax: Decreased (Vmax/α')
- Lineweaver-Burk: Parallel lines (same slope)
- Overcome by substrate? No

**Irreversible Inhibition**
- Binds: Active site (covalent bond)
- Km: Unchanged
- Vmax: Decreased
- Lineweaver-Burk: Higher y-intercept, same x-intercept
- Overcome by substrate? No

---

## Reading Lineweaver-Burk Plots: A Step-by-Step Strategy

When an MCAT passage presents a Lineweaver-Burk plot with and without inhibitor, use this systematic approach:

**Step 1: Compare y-intercepts.**
- Same y-intercept → Vmax unchanged → *competitive* inhibition
- Higher y-intercept → Vmax decreased → noncompetitive, uncompetitive, or irreversible

**Step 2: Compare x-intercepts.**
- Same x-intercept → Km unchanged → noncompetitive or irreversible
- x-intercept shifted right (less negative) → apparent Km decreased → *uncompetitive*
- x-intercept shifted left (more negative) → apparent Km increased → *competitive*

**Step 3: Compare slopes.**
- Parallel lines (same slope) → *uncompetitive*
- Lines intersect at y-axis → *competitive*
- Lines intersect at x-axis → *noncompetitive*

**Step 4: Cross-check with the Km/Vmax story.**
- If Vmax decreases and Km decreases by the same factor → uncompetitive
- If Vmax decreases and Km is unchanged → noncompetitive
- If Vmax unchanged and Km increases → competitive

This four-step approach handles every Lineweaver-Burk question the MCAT can generate.

---

## Allosteric Regulation vs. Inhibition

A common point of confusion is distinguishing enzyme inhibition from **allosteric regulation**. Both involve molecules binding to enzymes and altering activity, but they differ in important ways:

- Allosteric regulation is a *physiological* control mechanism using endogenous molecules (metabolites, second messengers). It often involves cooperative binding and sigmoidal kinetics rather than Michaelis-Menten hyperbolic kinetics.
- Inhibition (as discussed here) typically refers to exogenous molecules (drugs, toxins) or feedback inhibitors acting on non-allosteric enzymes.
- Many allosteric inhibitors are *noncompetitive* in their kinetic behavior, but not all noncompetitive inhibitors are allosteric regulators in the physiological sense.

**Feedback inhibition** is a specific form of allosteric inhibition where the *end product* of a metabolic pathway inhibits an early enzyme in that pathway. For example, in the isoleucine biosynthesis pathway, isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase (the first enzyme in the pathway) when isoleucine levels are high. This is typically noncompetitive or mixed inhibition kinetically.

---

## Calculating Ki and Quantitative Applications

The MCAT occasionally requires quantitative reasoning about inhibition constants. Here are the essential relationships:

For competitive inhibition, the apparent Km under inhibition:
- αKm = Km(1 + [I]/Ki)
- If you know uninhibited Km, inhibited apparent Km, and [I], you can solve for Ki

For noncompetitive inhibition, the apparent Vmax under inhibition:
- Vmax(apparent) = Vmax/(1 + [I]/Ki)
- If you know uninhibited Vmax, inhibited Vmax, and [I], you can solve for Ki

**Example:** An enzyme has Km = 2 mM and Vmax = 100 μmol/min. In the presence of 5 μM inhibitor, the apparent Km rises to 6 mM while Vmax remains 100 μmol/min. What type of inhibitor is this, and what is Ki?

- Vmax unchanged, Km increased → *competitive inhibitor*
- α = apparent Km / Km = 6/2 = 3
- α = 1 + [I]/Ki → 3 = 1 + 5/Ki → Ki = 2.5 μM

A Ki of 2.5 μM means the inhibitor has high affinity for the enzyme—this is typical of clinically useful competitive inhibitors.

---

## Integration with Broader Biochemistry

### pH and Temperature as "Inhibitors"

While not classical inhibitors, extreme pH and temperature alter enzyme activity in ways that mimic inhibition. Denaturation at high temperature or pH extremes outside the enzyme's optimum (typically pH 6–8 for most enzymes, pH 2 for pepsin, pH 8 for trypsin) reduces Vmax by destroying enzyme structure. These effects are generally irreversible at extreme conditions.

### Prodrugs and Inhibition

Some drugs are administered as inactive **prodrugs** that are converted by enzymes into active inhibitors. This is relevant to MCAT pharmacology passages. For example, many organophosphate pesticides are prodrugs activated by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes to their active, acetylcholinesterase-inhibiting forms.

### Enzyme Inhibition in Metabolic Pathways

Understanding inhibition types helps predict metabolic consequences:
- **Competitive inhibition** of a pathway enzyme can be overcome by substrate accumulation upstream—the pathway slows but doesn't stop.
- **Noncompetitive or irreversible inhibition** cannot be overcome; the pathway is blocked regardless of substrate levels.
- This distinction matters clinically: some toxins (cyanide, carbon monoxide) are noncompetitive/irreversible inhibitors of critical enzymes, making them lethal even when substrates are abundant.

---

## High-Yield MCAT Facts to Memorize

- **Competitive**: Km ↑, Vmax unchanged; lines meet at y-axis; overcome by [S]↑
- **Noncompetitive**: Km unchanged, Vmax ↓; lines meet at x-axis; NOT overcome by [S]↑
- **Uncompetitive**: Km ↓, Vmax ↓ (same factor); parallel lines; NOT overcome by [S]↑
- **Irreversible**: Vmax ↓, Km unchanged; permanent; requires new enzyme synthesis
- The **α factor** (1 + [I]/Ki) scales Km upward in competitive inhibition
- The **α' factor** (1 + [I]/Ki') scales both Km and Vmax downward equally in uncompetitive inhibition
- Aspirin → irreversible COX inhibition; Statins → competitive HMG-CoA reductase inhibition; Cyanide → noncompetitive cytochrome c oxidase inhibition
- Parallel lines on Lineweaver-Burk = *always* uncompetitive
- Lines crossing on y-axis = *always* competitive
- Lines crossing on x-axis = *always* pure noncompetitive

---

## Practice Question

**Question:** An enzyme catalyzes the conversion of substrate S to product P. In the absence of inhibitor, Km = 4 mM and Vmax = 80 nmol/min. When 10 nM of inhibitor X is added, Km appears to be 2 mM and Vmax appears to be 40 nmol/min. What type of inhibitor is X?

**Analysis:**
- Km decreased from 4 mM to 2 mM → apparent Km decreased
- Vmax decreased from 80 to 40 nmol/min → Vmax decreased
- Ratio: Km decreased by factor of 2; Vmax decreased by factor of 2 → same factor
- Conclusion: **Uncompetitive inhibitor**

Verification: α' = Vmax/Vmax(apparent) = 80/40 = 2; Km/α' = 4/2 = 2 mM ✓

On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the inhibited and uninhibited lines would be parallel.

---

## Conclusion

Enzyme inhibition is not merely an abstract biochemical concept—it is the mechanistic foundation of pharmacology and toxicology. The MCAT tests this topic because understanding how drugs and toxins alter enzyme kinetics requires integrating molecular structure, binding equilibria, and graphical data interpretation simultaneously.

The core framework is simple: *where does the inhibitor bind, and does substrate competition matter?* Competitive inhibitors fight substrate for the active site, raising Km but leaving Vmax intact—and substrate can win. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and reduce Vmax regardless of substrate—substrate cannot win. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only to the ES complex, reducing both Km and Vmax equally—more substrate actually worsens inhibition. Irreversible inhibitors form covalent bonds, permanently reducing functional enzyme concentration.

Master the Lineweaver-Burk signatures, understand the molecular logic behind each Km and Vmax change, and connect each inhibition type to its clinical archetype. With that framework, any MCAT question on enzyme inhibition becomes a pattern-matching exercise rather than a memory test.

questions.question_text: A researcher studies an enzyme with a Km of 2 mM and Vmax of 100 nmol/min. After adding inhibitor X, the apparent Km increases to 6 mM while Vmax remains 100 nmol/min. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
questions.choice_a: Inhibitor X is a noncompetitive inhibitor that binds the enzyme-substrate complex.
questions.choice_b: Inhibitor X is a competitive inhibitor that can be displaced by increasing substrate concentration.
questions.choice_c: Inhibitor X is an uncompetitive inhibitor that lowers both Km and Vmax.
questions.choice_d: Inhibitor X is an irreversible inhibitor that permanently blocks the active site.
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors increase apparent Km (reflecting reduced substrate affinity) while leaving Vmax unchanged because excess substrate can outcompete the inhibitor for the active site. The threefold increase in Km with no change in Vmax is the hallmark of competitive inhibition. Noncompetitive inhibition would decrease Vmax without changing Km, and uncompetitive inhibition would decrease both Km and Vmax proportionally. Irreversible inhibitors would permanently reduce Vmax and cannot be overcome by substrate.

questions.question_text: On a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot, an inhibitor causes a family of lines that all intersect at the same point on the y-axis but have different slopes. What type of inhibition does this pattern indicate?
questions.explanation: In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax and the x-intercept equals -1/Km. Competitive inhibitors increase Km (changing the slope) but do not alter Vmax, so lines intersect at the same y-intercept with different slopes. Noncompetitive inhibitors change the y-intercept (reduced Vmax) while lines intersect on the x-axis. Uncompetitive inhibitors produce parallel lines with the same slope but different intercepts. Mixed inhibition changes both intercepts.

questions.question_text: An enzyme inhibitor binds only to the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex and not to the free enzyme. Which of the following correctly describes the kinetic effect of this inhibitor?
questions.choice_c: Vmax is unchanged and Km increases.
questions.choice_d: Vmax increases and Km is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind exclusively to the ES complex, stabilizing it and preventing product formation. This lowers Vmax because fewer productive complexes form. Paradoxically, Km also decreases because binding of the inhibitor to ES effectively pulls the equilibrium toward ES formation, making the enzyme appear to have higher affinity for substrate. This proportional decrease in both Km and Vmax is the defining feature of uncompetitive inhibition. Competitive inhibition raises Km without changing Vmax, making choice C a common distractor.

questions.question_text: A pharmaceutical company tests a new drug that reduces enzyme Vmax by 50% regardless of substrate concentration, while the Km remains unchanged. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, lines generated with and without the drug would most likely:
questions.choice_a: Intersect at the x-axis, showing the same -1/Km value.
questions.choice_b: Be parallel, showing the same slope but different y-intercepts.
questions.choice_c: Intersect at the y-axis, showing the same 1/Vmax value.
questions.choice_d: Intersect at the origin, indicating no net change in catalysis.
questions.explanation: Pure noncompetitive inhibition decreases Vmax without affecting Km. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, unchanged Km means the x-intercept (-1/Km) is the same for both lines, so they intersect on the x-axis. The y-intercept (1/Vmax) increases as Vmax decreases, so the inhibited line has a higher y-intercept and steeper slope. Parallel lines are characteristic of uncompetitive inhibition. Intersecting at the y-axis would indicate competitive inhibition, where Vmax is unchanged.

questions.question_text: A student compares two enzyme inhibitors. Inhibitor A increases the apparent Km fourfold with no change in Vmax. Inhibitor B decreases Vmax by half and also decreases Km by half. If substrate concentration is raised to a very high level (saturating), which inhibitor will most impair enzyme activity?
questions.choice_a: Inhibitor A, because it has a greater effect on substrate binding.
questions.choice_b: Inhibitor B, because its effect on Vmax cannot be overcome by substrate.
questions.choice_c: Both inhibitors equally, because both reduce overall catalytic efficiency.
questions.choice_d: Neither inhibitor, because saturating substrate always restores full Vmax.
questions.explanation: At saturating substrate concentrations, competitive inhibitors (like Inhibitor A) are outcompeted, and Vmax is fully restored; the increase in Km becomes irrelevant. Uncompetitive inhibitors (like Inhibitor B) bind only to the ES complex, so more substrate actually drives more ES formation and more inhibitor binding, meaning Vmax remains reduced at all substrate concentrations and cannot be rescued by excess substrate. Therefore, Inhibitor B will continue to impair enzyme activity even at saturating substrate levels.
